title: Where the Arm Can Work: Reach by Sampling, the Shorter Reach With the Tool Down, the Smaller Region Where It Can Move Well, and What Fits on a Table

questions.question: How do you find the reach of an arm by sampling?
options: Solve the inverse kinematics on a grid of poses
Draw random joint angles, run forward kinematics and mark the cell of the tool
Sweep each joint in turn with the others fixed
questions.explanation: Random angles inside the limits, forward kinematics, and a mark in the cell the tool lands in. It needs no inverse and no guess at the shape.

questions.question: With 2 thousand poses the volume was how much against 200 thousand?
questions.explanation: Places near the edge are reached by very few combinations of angles, so a small sample misses them. A count still rising with the sample is not yet a volume.

questions.question: How far out at table height did the tool reach in any orientation, and pointing down?
questions.explanation: Asking for the tool to point down uses up some of the arm. That 0.12 m is the gap between the data sheet's reach and the task's.

questions.question: What share of the reachable volume were the dexterous poses?
questions.explanation: The rest is reachable but close to a singularity: the arm can be put there and cannot then move well in every direction.

questions.question: Why does a table need the joint limits in the question?
options: The closed form fails without limits
The closed form gives all the solutions; the arm can take only those inside its limits: 96 percent against 78 with plus and minus 60 degrees
questions.explanation: Limits of 120 degrees cost nothing here, which was measured and not assumed. Limits of 60 degrees took the coverage from 96 to 78 percent.

questions.question: Why is the reach on a data sheet not the working area?
options: It is the outside of a sphere; the useful region is shorter once the orientation is asked for and smaller where the arm cannot move well
It is measured with no payload
It is rounded up by the maker
It is given for the flange and not the tool
questions.explanation: Reach is the furthest the tool gets in any orientation. With the tool pointing down, and only where the arm still moves well, the region is smaller.
